overview.text: The retina is the light-sensitive, layered neural tissue lining the back of the eyeball. The eye focuses light onto it, where rods and cones—its photoreceptor cells—begin the process of turning light into signals. Rods respond to dim light, while cones help detect color. Other retinal neurons process and relay this information; axons of retinal ganglion cells join to form the optic nerve, which carries signals to the brain. The macula, a central area of the retina, supports central vision, and its center, the fovea, provides the sharpest vision. The retina is essential to sight because it starts and organizes the eye’s visual signals.

key_facts.text: The retina lines the back of the eyeball and sends electrical impulses through the optic nerve to the brain.
Rods are specialized for dim light; cones are specialized for brighter light and color.
Retinal ganglion cell axons converge and leave the eye as the optic nerve.
The macula is a small retinal area needed for central vision; the fovea at its center is where vision is sharpest.
The retina is made up of interconnected neurons that encode light into signals the brain can understand.
